summary: Psalm 57 begins with a speaker asking God for mercy while taking refuge from disaster and pursuit. The poem moves through danger described as lions, weapons, a net, and a pit, then turns toward a steadfast heart, public thanksgiving, and a repeated call for God’s glory to be over all the earth.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how a prayer of danger can become praise without pretending the danger is imaginary. Within Psalms, it belongs to the many poems that hold fear, trust, enemy pressure, and worship in one voiced prayer.

context.author: The heading associates the poem with David, “when he fled from Saul, in the cave”; Psalms headings are ancient features of the collection, though readers differ on whether such headings identify authorship, association, dedication, or later placement.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities receiving it as Scripture and prayer.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 57 is uncertain.
context.setting: Book II of Psalms, in a David-associated prayer that names crisis, pursuit, and refuge in God.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with a musical heading, repeated refrain, vivid images, and “Selah” as a preserved performance marker of uncertain force.

outline.heading: Mercy and refuge
outline.note: The speaker asks God for mercy, takes refuge under God’s wings, cries to God Most High, and expects God to save and send loving kindness and truth.

outline.heading: Danger among enemies
outline.note: The threat is pictured as lions, fire, spears, arrows, and a sharp sword-like tongue.

outline.heading: First refrain of glory
outline.note: The prayer widens from personal danger to God being exalted above heaven and earth.

outline.heading: The trap reverses
outline.note: The enemies prepare a net and dig a pit, but the poem says they fall into it themselves.

outline.heading: Steadfast praise
outline.note: The speaker’s heart is steadfast, instruments are awakened, and thanksgiving is promised among peoples and nations because God’s loving kindness and truth reach upward.

outline.heading: Final refrain of glory
outline.note: The psalm closes by repeating the call for God to be exalted above the heavens and for God’s glory to cover the earth.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A poem by David, when he fled from Saul, in the cave. Be merciful to me, God, be merciful to me, for my soul takes refuge in you. Yes, in the shadow of your wings, I will take refuge, until disaster has passed.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the poem’s musical and David-associated heading, then states the central posture: urgent need and refuge in God.

keyVerses.text: Be exalted, God, above the heavens! Let your glory be above all the earth!
keyVerses.why: This refrain interrupts the crisis with a larger horizon: the speaker wants God’s honor recognized beyond the immediate danger.

keyVerses.text: My heart is steadfast, God. My heart is steadfast. I will sing, yes, I will sing praises.
keyVerses.why: The poem turns from bowed-down distress to resolved praise, making this verse a hinge in the chapter.

keyVerses.text: For your great loving kindness reaches to the heavens, and your truth to the skies.
keyVerses.why: This gives the reason for the praise in verses 7-9: God’s loving kindness and truth are pictured as vast and high-reaching.

themes: God’s glory over earth and heavens

questions.question: What does the heading tell a reader before the prayer begins?
questions.answer: The heading gives musical and traditional framing: it names the Chief Musician, the tune “Do Not Destroy,” and calls the psalm “A poem by David” connected with flight from Saul in a cave. Psalms headings may mark authorship, association, dedication, collection, or remembered setting, so the heading should be treated as evidence without pretending it answers every historical question.

questions.question: Why does the speaker repeat “be merciful to me”?
questions.answer: The repetition makes the plea urgent. Verse 1 does not explain every detail of the disaster, but it shows the speaker asking God for mercy while choosing refuge “in the shadow of your wings” until the danger passes.

questions.question: What does “God Most High” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse it is a title used while crying out to God for help. The next phrase, “to God who accomplishes my requests for me,” shows that the speaker is appealing to God as the one able to act on his behalf.

questions.question: What is “Selah”?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears in verses 3 and 6. Translations often preserve the Hebrew sound because its exact performance instruction is no longer known, so it signals the poem’s voiced or musical setting without letting us reconstruct the precise ancient practice.

questions.question: Are the enemies literal lions?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says, “My soul is among lions,” then immediately describes “the sons of men” with teeth like spears and arrows and a tongue like a sharp sword. The verse itself points readers toward poetic imagery for dangerous people, especially people whose speech harms.

questions.question: Why does the psalm ask for God to be exalted above the heavens while the speaker is still in trouble?
questions.answer: The refrain in verse 5 does not wait until every threat is gone. It places the speaker’s crisis inside a bigger claim about God’s glory over heaven and earth, and the same refrain returns at the end after the movement into praise.

questions.question: What happens to the net and pit prepared by the enemies?
questions.answer: Verse 6 says the enemies prepared a net and dug a pit, but then “They fall into the middle of it themselves.” The verse presents a reversal: the danger meant for the speaker turns back on those who set it.

questions.question: How does the poem move from fear to praise?
questions.answer: The speaker begins with mercy, refuge, pursuit, and disaster in verses 1-3, and describes severe threat in verses 4 and 6. By verse 7 the speaker says his heart is steadfast and chooses song, then promises thanksgiving among peoples and nations in verse 9.

questions.question: Does “among the peoples” and “among the nations” mean the whole poem is public?
questions.answer: The earlier verses sound intensely personal, with “my soul,” “my requests,” and “my heart.” Verse 9 widens that personal prayer into public thanksgiving beyond the speaker’s own immediate setting, but the chapter itself does not describe when or how that public praise takes place.

glossary.def: A place of safety. In this psalm the speaker says his soul takes refuge in God and repeats that he will take refuge under God’s wings until disaster has passed.
A preserved performance marker in the Psalms. Its exact instruction is uncertain, so it should be noticed without overexplaining it.
A translation used here for God’s faithful mercy or loyal care. In this chapter God sends it in verse 3, and it reaches to the heavens in verse 10.
A word paired with “loving kindness” in verses 3 and 10. The psalm presents it as something God sends and as something reaching “to the skies.”
A musical instrument named in verse 8 when the speaker calls for praise to wake up.
A musical instrument named with the lute in verse 8 as the poem turns toward song.
